claims.text: Pre-forming a thin, continuous alumina layer on boride-based components will reduce their corrosion rate in molten aluminum.
Heating the boride alloy in an oxygen-containing atmosphere can develop an in situ Al2O3 surface layer.
Typical hot-dip aluminum-plating exposure temperatures are approximately 700–800 °C.
The pre-oxidation treatment forms a thin, coherent alumina barrier on the component surface.
The alumina layer acts as a diffusion barrier.
The alumina barrier inhibits dissolution of underlying boride-substrate elements into molten aluminum.
The alumina barrier minimizes interfacial reactions between the substrate and molten aluminum.
The alumina barrier prevents penetration of aluminum into the substrate.
Inhibiting dissolution, interfacial reactions, and aluminum penetration reduces corrosion.
Pre-oxidized components will have significantly lower mass loss than untreated boride components under identical molten-aluminum exposure.
Pre-oxidized components will exhibit less surface degradation than untreated boride components under identical molten-aluminum exposure.
Untreated boride-based components are expected to corrode faster than components bearing the proposed alumina layer.
The protective benefit depends on the continuity, thickness, adhesion, and stability of the alumina layer.
A nonuniform or unstable alumina coating will diminish the protective effect.
Spallation of the alumina layer during processing will diminish its protective effect.
The magnitude of corrosion-rate reduction may depend on pre-oxidation temperature, duration, and atmospheric composition.
Alumina provides protective benefits in high-temperature environments.
The long-term stability of alumina in dynamic molten-aluminum systems remains to be quantitatively determined.
